title: Space, density and level of service
summary: Density is people per square metre; its inverse is the space each person has. Fruin's levels of service turn space per person into grades from A (free) to F (breakdown).
outcomes: calculate density and space per person from a count and an area
read a level of service from A to F
explain why the same number of people can be fine in one place and dangerous in another
estimate how many people fit in an area at a chosen comfort level
narration_en: How full is a space? Crowd scientists answer with one number: density, the number of people per square metre. Count the people in an area and divide by the area. Turn it upside down and you get the space each person has. At one person per square metre you can walk freely. At two, you have to adjust your speed and path. At four, you are shuffling and brushing against others. At six or more, you are pressed by bodies on all sides and cannot move on your own. In the nineteen seventies the engineer John Fruin turned these experiences into levels of service, graded from A, free movement, to F, where flow breaks down. Planners still use them to design walkways, platforms and queues. In this module you will measure density, read levels of service, and estimate how many people a space can hold comfortably. Remember: the same thousand people are comfortable in a large square and dangerous in a narrow street.
narration_ar: ما مدى امتلاء مكان ما؟ يجيب علماء الحشود برقم واحد: الكثافة، أي عدد الأشخاص في كل متر مربع. عُدّ الناس في منطقة ما واقسم العدد على المساحة. واقلب الكسر تحصل على المساحة المتاحة لكل شخص. عند شخص واحد في المتر المربع تستطيع أن تمشي بحرية. وعند شخصين عليك أن تعدّل سرعتك ومسارك. وعند أربعة تمشي بخطوات قصيرة وتحتك بالآخرين. وعند ستة أو أكثر تضغطك الأجساد من كل جانب ولا تستطيع أن تتحرك وحدك. وفي سبعينيات القرن العشرين حوّل المهندس جون فروين هذه التجارب إلى مستويات خدمة، متدرجة من A، أي الحركة الحرة، إلى F حيث ينهار التدفق. وما زال المخططون يستخدمونها لتصميم الممرات والأرصفة وطوابير الانتظار. ستقيس في هذه الوحدة الكثافة، وتقرأ مستويات الخدمة، وتقدّر كم شخصاً يتسع له مكان ما براحة. وتذكّر: الألف شخص نفسهم مرتاحون في ساحة كبيرة، ومعرّضون للخطر في شارع ضيق.

diagram.title: From a count to a level of service
diagram.caption: Density = people ÷ area. Space per person is its inverse. Levels of service grade space per person from A to F.

nodes.label: Count
nodes.detail: Count everyone inside a known area, from the ground, a photo or a sensor.

nodes.label: Area
nodes.detail: Use the area people can actually stand or walk in: subtract barriers, columns and stalls.

nodes.label: Density
nodes.detail: Density ρ = count ÷ area. One person per m² is comfortable walking; six or more is dangerous.

nodes.label: Space per person
nodes.detail: The inverse of density. Fruin's grades use space per person.

nodes.label: Level of service
nodes.detail: Walkway levels (Fruin 1971): A more than 3.25 m² each, B 2.3–3.25, C 1.4–2.3, D 0.9–1.4, E 0.5–0.9, F under 0.5.

nodes.label: Holding capacity
nodes.detail: To find how many fit at a comfort level, multiply the usable area by the density you accept.

tour.text: Start with a count and an area. Use only the area people can really use.
Density is the count divided by the area: people per square metre.
Turn it upside down for the space each person has.
Fruin graded that space from A to F. A is free walking; F is where flow breaks down.
Planners run it backwards: choose a grade, then area × density tells you how many people fit.

rows.name: C
rows.purpose: 1.4–2.3 m² each: speed and passing restricted

rows.name: F
rows.purpose: Under 0.5 m² each: frequent contact, flow breaks down

sections.heading: Density, the key number
sections.html:
Density is the number of people per square metre, written ρ (rho). Count the people in a known area and divide:

ρ = number of people ÷ area (people per m²)

Example: 120 people in a 60 m² lobby give ρ = 2 people per m². The space per person is the inverse: 60 ÷ 120 = 0.5 m² each.

sections.heading: What density feels like
sections.html: Rough guide, for adults moving in one direction: below 1 per m² you walk freely; about 2 you adjust speed and path; about 4 you shuffle with frequent contact; above about 5 to 6 you cannot move independently and pressure can build (Fruin 1993; Still 2014). Standing still, people tolerate higher densities than walking, which is why queues and viewing areas use different thresholds.

sections.heading: Levels of service
sections.html: John Fruin (1971) graded walkways A to F by space per person, like grades on a report card. Designers choose a target grade for the busiest 15 minutes, often C or D for stations and B or C for comfortable public spaces. Separate scales exist for queuing areas and stairs, because standing and climbing need different space.

sections.heading: How many people fit?
sections.html: Run the calculation backwards. A 2,000 m² square, of which 1,600 m² is usable, at a comfortable 2 people per m² holds 3,200 people. At 4 per m² it holds 6,400, but people can no longer move freely. Remember that density is never even: people gather near stages, exits and screens, so average density hides dangerous hot spots.

callouts.title: Quick check
callouts.html: A platform is 100 m long and 4 m wide, and 600 people wait on it. Density? 600 ÷ 400 = 1.5 per m², about 0.67 m² each: level E for a walkway, tolerable for waiting.

callouts.title: Average density
callouts.html: 'The square was only half full' can still hide 6 per m² at the front. Always ask where the people were, not just how many.

takeaways: Density ρ = people ÷ area; space per person = 1 ÷ ρ.
Below about 1 per m² people walk freely; above about 5–6 per m² they cannot move independently.
Fruin's levels of service grade space per person from A to F.
Holding capacity = usable area × accepted density, but averages hide hot spots.

quiz.q: 200 people stand in a 50 m² area. What is the density?
At 2 people per m², how much space does each person have?
Fruin's level of service F means…
quiz.explain: F is under about 0.5 m² per person, where movement breaks down.

quiz.q: Why can an average density be misleading?
options: People cluster at hot spots like stage fronts and exits
quiz.explain: Crowds are uneven; danger is local.

glossary.def: Number of people per square metre (ρ).
Area available to each person, the inverse of density, in m².
A grade (A to F) of crowd comfort based on space per person or flow (Fruin 1971).
The number of people an area can hold at an accepted density.
The area people can actually occupy, excluding obstacles.
